about.title: About Bahia Palace
about.body: Built in the late 19th century for Si Moussa, grand vizier of the sultan, Bahia Palace ("Palace of the Beautiful") is a masterpiece of Moroccan architecture. Its 8 hectares of intricate zellige tilework, carved cedar ceilings, and lush gardens have enchanted visitors for over a century.

items.question: Is Bahia Palace worth visiting in 2026?
items.answer: Absolutely. Bahia Palace is one of the best-preserved examples of 19th-century Moroccan architecture. With 150 rooms, intricate zellige tilework, hand-painted cedar ceilings, and lush inner gardens, it offers an unmatched glimpse into Moroccan royal life. Most visitors rate it as the highlight of their Marrakech trip. At 100 MAD (≈ €9.90), it's exceptional value — and with a skip-the-line ticket, the experience becomes completely seamless.

items.question: How much does Bahia Palace cost to enter?
items.answer: The official gate entrance fee is 100 MAD (about €9.90). Children under 7 enter free, and children aged 7–13 pay 50 MAD. Booked online with us you get — the official ticket, a multilingual audio guide and support — and it means you skip the ticket-office queue, which can reach 1–2 hours in peak season.

items.question: How long do you need at Bahia Palace?
items.answer: Most visitors spend 1 to 1.5 hours exploring independently. With a guided tour, expect 1.5 to 2 hours. Private tours are flexible and can last up to 2.5 hours. We recommend arriving early (9–10 AM) to enjoy the space without crowds.

items.question: When is the best time to visit Bahia Palace?
items.answer: The best time is 9:00–10:30 AM when the palace first opens — fewest visitors and soft morning light ideal for photography. Avoid 10:30 AM–2:00 PM when tour groups arrive in force. Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–November) offer the most pleasant temperatures at 20–28°C.

items.question: Is Bahia Palace free to enter?
items.answer: Bahia Palace is not free for adult visitors. The entrance fee is 100 MAD (≈ €9.90). Children under 7 enter free, and children aged 7–13 pay 50 MAD (≈ €4.95). Photography is included in the ticket price with no extra charges.

items.question: How do I get to Bahia Palace from Jemaa el-Fnaa?
items.answer: Bahia Palace is a 10–15 minute walk south from Jemaa el-Fnaa through the medina. Follow the signs for 'Palais Bahia' or use Google Maps. A petit taxi takes about 5 minutes and costs 15–25 MAD. The palace address is Rue Riad Zitoun el Jedid, Marrakech Medina.

items.question: Are guided tours worth it at Bahia Palace?
items.answer: Yes, especially for a first visit. Bahia Palace has 150 rooms and historical layers that are invisible without explanation. A guide will tell you about Ba Ahmed's political rise, why the palace was looted overnight after his death in 1900, and identify architectural details most visitors walk past. Guided tours are coming soon — contact us to be notified when they launch.

items.question: What is Bahia Palace famous for?
items.answer: Bahia Palace is famous for its extraordinary Moroccan craftsmanship — particularly the hand-cut zellige tile mosaics, elaborately carved stucco plasterwork, and painted cedar wood ceilings. It is one of the largest palaces in Marrakech at 8 hectares with 150 rooms. Built by Grand Vizier Ba Ahmed between 1894 and 1900.

items.question: Can you visit Bahia Palace without a guide?
items.answer: Yes, Bahia Palace can be visited independently. Most visitors explore comfortably in 1–1.5 hours at their own pace. No official audio guide is available on-site, so booking a guided tour is recommended if you want the full story.

items.question: Is Bahia Palace suitable for children?
items.answer: Yes, Bahia Palace is very family-friendly. Children under 7 enter free. The open courtyards, colourful tiles, and garden spaces fascinate younger visitors. The grounds are mostly flat and accessible with a pushchair or wheelchair.

items.question: What should I wear at Bahia Palace?
items.answer: Bahia Palace does not enforce a strict dress code, but modest attire is respectful and recommended. Covering shoulders and knees is appropriate. Comfortable walking shoes are essential — the floors mix polished marble, zellige tiles, and stone, which can be slippery.

items.question: Is photography allowed inside Bahia Palace?
items.answer: Yes, photography is freely allowed throughout Bahia Palace for personal use at no extra charge. The best light for photography is early morning (9–10:30 AM). Tripods and professional equipment require prior authorisation.

items.question: How do I book skip-the-line tickets for Bahia Palace online?
items.answer: Click 'Get Tickets' on this page to be redirected to the official Ministry of Culture ticketing portal (e-services.minculture.gov.ma), where you can select your date, number of guests, and complete your purchase directly. Your QR code ticket will be emailed by the official portal.

items.question: Can I cancel or change my Bahia Palace ticket?
items.answer: Cancellation policy is set by the official portal where you complete your purchase (e-services.minculture.gov.ma) — check the terms shown there at checkout. We don't process payments, so we can't offer cancellations ourselves.

items.question: What else is near Bahia Palace?
items.answer: The Saadian Tombs are just a 7-minute walk — stunning 16th-century royal mausoleums. El Badi Palace ruins are 10 minutes on foot. Jemaa el-Fnaa square is a 15-minute walk north. Most visitors combine Bahia Palace with the Saadian Tombs in a half-day.

items.question: Can you buy Bahia Palace tickets at the door?
items.answer: Yes, tickets can be purchased at the entrance gate in cash (Moroccan dirhams only — no cards accepted). However, queues can reach 45–90 minutes during peak season (March–May, October–November) and on weekends. Buying skip-the-line tickets online in advance guarantees your entry time and bypasses the queue entirely — especially important for morning slots.

items.question: Is Bahia Palace free on Fridays?
items.answer: No, Bahia Palace is not free on Fridays for tourists. The entrance fee of 100 MAD applies every day of the week. Free admission applies only to Moroccan nationals on specific national and religious holidays. There is no reduced or free entry for foreign visitors on any day, including Fridays.

items.question: What are Bahia Palace opening hours in 2026?
items.answer: Bahia Palace is open daily from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (last entry 4:30 PM). Hours vary during Ramadan — typically 9:30 AM to 3:00 PM. The palace is open every day of the year including weekends and most public holidays, though hours may be reduced on major religious holidays. We recommend arriving at opening time (9 AM) to avoid the worst of the crowds.

items.question: Is Bahia Palace wheelchair accessible?
items.answer: Yes, most of Bahia Palace is accessible for wheelchair users and visitors with reduced mobility. The main courtyards, gardens, and principal rooms have smooth paved surfaces. A few inner chambers have small raised thresholds. Pushchairs and prams navigate the palace comfortably. The main entrance has a ramped access route. If you need assistance, palace staff can help at the entrance.

items.question: Bahia Palace or Majorelle Garden — which should I visit?
items.answer: They offer completely different experiences. Bahia Palace is 19th-century Moroccan royal architecture: carved plaster, zellige tile mosaics, painted cedar ceilings, and the fascinating story of Grand Vizier Ba Ahmed. Majorelle Garden is a botanical garden with Art Déco architecture and the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Most visitors do both in a single day (they are 25 minutes apart by taxi). If you must choose one: pick Bahia Palace for Moroccan history and architecture, or Majorelle if you prefer gardens and fashion/design.

safetyGuide.title: Visit Marrakech Smart — Avoid the Common Scams
safetyGuide.subtitle: Marrakech is a wonderful city. Like any major tourist destination, it has a small number of scams targeting visitors. Know them before you go — and enjoy your trip with confidence.
safetyGuide.ctaBody: The safest way to buy Bahia Palace tickets is directly online — before you arrive. No street vendors, no "official" touts at the entrance.
safetyGuide.contributeBody: Help other travellers by sharing your experience. WhatsApp us and we'll add it to this guide (anonymously).

scams.title: The "Closed Monument" Trick
scams.desc: A stranger approaches and tells you the palace is closed today for a private event, holiday, or renovation — but offers to take you to an "equally beautiful" alternative.
scams.avoid: Ignore them. Bahia Palace is open daily 9 AM–5 PM. Check the official website. Walk directly to the entrance.

scams.title: Fake Guides at the Entrance
scams.desc: People standing near the entrance offering unofficial tours, often insisting they are official or licensed. They may demand large sums at the end.
scams.avoid: Book your guide through our platform in advance. Official guides wear a badge issued by the regional tourist board.

scams.title: The Henna Ambush
scams.desc: A woman in Jemaa el-Fna or narrow streets grabs your hand and begins applying henna without asking. When done, she demands €20–50 for it.
scams.avoid: Keep your hands to yourself in busy areas. If approached, firmly say "No thank you" and keep walking.

scams.title: Taxi Without a Meter
scams.desc: Drivers agree on a fare verbally, then claim they said a much higher price on arrival, or take a longer route to inflate the cost.
scams.avoid: Always insist the driver use the meter (compteur). Agree on a price before getting in. Use Careem or inDrive apps for transparent pricing.

scams.title: The "I'll Show You the Way" Pickpocket
scams.desc: A friendly local offers to show you to a nearby landmark. While walking through narrow alleys, an accomplice pickpockets you.
scams.avoid: Download offline maps (Maps.me or Google Maps) before exploring. Politely decline unsolicited guides.

scams.title: Overpriced Spice Shops
scams.desc: A "guide" takes you to a spice shop where items are massively overpriced and you feel pressured to buy.
scams.avoid: Avoid following anyone into shops. Prices in the souk are negotiable — start at 30–40% of the asking price.

scams.title: Fake Tannery Viewpoint
scams.desc: You're told a viewpoint over the famous tanneries is "free" — but you must enter through a leather shop and are pressured to buy.
scams.avoid: This is normal for the tanneries — you do pass through shops. Just be firm: look, smell the mint, and say you're not buying.

scams.title: Snake Charmer Photo Trap
scams.desc: Snake charmers in Jemaa el-Fna place a snake or monkey on you and demand €10–30 for a photo you didn't ask for.
scams.avoid: Do not stand near snake charmers unless you intend to pay. Keep your camera in your bag in that area.

scams.title: Currency Exchange Confusion
scams.desc: Informal money changers offer great rates but use sleight of hand to shortchange you, or give you old/void notes.
scams.avoid: Only exchange money at official bank branches or ATMs. Never use street money changers.

scams.title: Restaurant Menu Switcheroo
scams.desc: You're shown a menu with low prices outside, then given a different menu inside, or charged far more than agreed.
scams.avoid: Check the menu carefully before sitting down. Ask to confirm prices before ordering. Pay by card if possible.

scams.title: Fake or Counterfeit Tickets
scams.desc: Tickets sold by someone standing near the entrance, or bought from a site that copies the look of an official one. They are cheap, they look real, and the gate refuses them — usually after you have queued.
scams.avoid: Buy before you arrive, from the Ministry portal or from a seller who names the company behind the sale. Nobody official sells tickets on the street outside Bahia Palace.

scams.title: The "Free" Gift
scams.desc: Someone presses a sprig of rosemary, a bracelet or a small trinket into your hand and calls it a gift. Once you are holding it, payment is demanded — loudly, and often with a small crowd gathering.
scams.avoid: Keep your hands down and say "la, shukran" without stopping. If you are already holding it, hand it straight back and keep walking. Nothing given away in the medina needs paying for later.

tips: Download offline maps before you arrive — GPS works without data.
Dress modestly in the medina — it reduces unwanted attention.
Keep a small amount of cash in a front pocket, the rest hidden.
Book tickets and tours online before arrival whenever possible.
If you feel followed, walk into any shop and ask for help.
Learn a few words of Arabic or Darija — locals deeply appreciate it.
Negotiate prices at the souk — it's expected and part of the culture.
Trust your instincts — if something feels wrong, walk away.
Use licensed taxis (petit taxi, cream-coloured) for safer rides.
Keep copies of your passport and insurance in a cloud service.

nearby.title: More to See Nearby
nearby.intro: Two more Marrakech monuments sit within a short walk of Bahia Palace. We publish an independent visitor guide for each of them.
nearby.badiBody: The roofless ruin of Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur's 16th-century showpiece — sunken orange gardens, vast reflecting pools and storks nesting on the ramparts. A 10-minute walk south of Bahia Palace, in the Kasbah.
nearby.saadianBody: The Saadian dynasty's royal necropolis, walled up for two centuries and rediscovered in 1917. The Hall of Twelve Columns holds some of Morocco's finest carved cedar and zellige. About 12 minutes on foot from Bahia Palace.

blogPreview.title: From the Visitor Guide
blogPreview.subtitle: Tips, history and practical advice for your visit to Bahia Palace

story.body: In 1866, the most powerful man in Morocco began building a palace for the woman he loved. He was Grand Vizier Ba Ahmed — and he named it Bahia: Arabic for "the brilliant one." He summoned the finest craftsmen from Fez, who spent decades carving cedar ceilings, hand-cutting zellige mosaics, and filling 150 rooms with interiors the likes of which Morocco had never seen. Ba Ahmed died in 1900. The palace has stood silent ever since — and still takes your breath away.

highlights.title: What you'll see
highlights.item1caption: Orange trees shade a courtyard where artisans once worked. Most visitors spend their first ten minutes here, just looking up.
highlights.item2caption: Artisans spent years on a single cedar ceiling. Every beam is different. None of it was touched by a machine.
highlights.item3caption: Each tile hand-cut and placed with precision. The geometry has no mistakes.
highlights.item4caption: The largest room in the palace — where Ba Ahmed received foreign dignitaries. The painted ceiling alone took artisans several years.

palaceHistory.h1: Bahia Palace History: Ba Ahmed and the Story Behind the Palace
palaceHistory.introA: Bahia Palace is not one building but two, forty years apart. The garden chambers carry an inscription dating them to {founded}, when the chamberlain Si Moussa built himself a house here. His son Ba Ahmed turned that house into the palace visitors walk through today between {expansion}, in the six years he governed Morocco in the name of a teenage sultan.
palaceHistory.introB: al-Bahia means “the brilliant”. It was reportedly the name of Ba Ahmed’s favourite wife, though some accounts read the name as describing the palace itself rather than a person.
palaceHistory.sourcedNote: Dates and figures on this page are sourced individually and listed in full under Sources.
palaceHistory.whoA: The palace was built in two phases. Si Moussa, chamberlain to Sultan {sultanMuhammad} and later grand vizier under {sultanHassan}, built the first house on the site. His son Ba Ahmed expanded it between {expansion}.
palaceHistory.whoB: Ba Ahmed did not inherit his father’s office. He served as hajib to {sultanHassan} from {hajibFrom}, and when the sultan died on campaign in {expansionFrom} he installed the {sultanAge}-year-old {sultanYoung} over his elder brothers and governed in his place until his own death.
palaceHistory.whoC: Ba Ahmed’s grandfather was enslaved, owned by Sultan {sultanSlimane}, and rose to become his hajib, or chamberlain. Ba Ahmed himself was born into an established makhzen family.
palaceHistory.whoD: The decoration was executed by Moroccan maalmin, principally Fez-trained specialists in zellige, gebs and cedar joinery. He assembled the ground by absorbing the plots of some {houses} neighbouring houses, with {gardens} gardens acquired for the grounds.
palaceHistory.srcInscription: Deverdun (1959), from the dated inscription in the two garden chambers
palaceHistory.srcChronicles: Contemporary Moroccan chronicles, summarised in Deverdun (1959)
palaceHistory.timelineTitle: Timeline: From a Private House to a World Heritage Site
palaceHistory.tl1Title: Si Moussa builds Dar Si Moussa
palaceHistory.tl1Text: The two chambers flanking the garden carry an inscription dating them to {founded}, the earliest firm date on the building. Si Moussa, chamberlain to Sultan {sultanMuhammad} and later grand vizier under {sultanHassan}, builds it as a private residence, not yet as Bahia.
palaceHistory.tl2Title: Ba Ahmed enters the household of {sultanHassan}
palaceHistory.tl2Text: Si Moussa’s son Ahmed ibn Moussa becomes hajib, chamberlain, to Sultan {sultanHassan}. He does not inherit his father’s vizierate; he builds his own position over the next fifteen years.
palaceHistory.tl3Text: {sultanHassan} dies on campaign. Ba Ahmed conceals the death long enough to install the {sultanAge}-year-old {sultanYoung} over his elder brothers, and becomes grand vizier and de facto regent. He begins expanding his father’s house into a palace.
palaceHistory.tl4Title: The palace takes its present shape
palaceHistory.tl4Text: Ba Ahmed absorbs the plots of some {houses} neighbouring houses and {gardens} gardens. The great marble courtyard is dated {marble} by inscription. The architect is {architect} of {architectFrom}.
palaceHistory.tl5Title: Death, and the stripping of the palace
palaceHistory.tl5Text: Ba Ahmed dies in Marrakesh. Sultan {sultanYoung} reportedly orders the palace looted of its valuables and the household expelled. The fixed decoration survives because it cannot be carried out.
palaceHistory.tl6Text: Under the French Protectorate the palace becomes the official residence of the resident-general, France’s representative in Morocco.
palaceHistory.tl7Text: The Medina of Marrakesh, the palace inside it, is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as entry {ref}. The palace is administered today by the Moroccan Ministry of Culture.
palaceHistory.archIntro: The decoration is Moroccan work in a style with deep Andalusi roots, executed by Fez-trained maalmin. The craftsmen were Moroccan, not imported from al-Andalus, which had ended four centuries earlier. Four trades account for almost everything a visitor sees.
palaceHistory.matZelligeDesc: Hand-cut glazed terracotta mosaic, laid across floors and lower walls.
palaceHistory.matGebsDesc: Carved gypsum plaster worked wet into arabesque and muqarnas panels.
palaceHistory.matCedarDesc: Middle Atlas cedar ceilings, carved and painted with mineral pigment.
palaceHistory.matMarbleDesc: Imported marble paving the great courtyard, dated {marble} by inscription.
palaceHistory.planTitle: See where all of this happened
palaceHistory.planBody: A schematic of the seven spaces in the order the visitor circuit takes you, with what happened in each.
palaceHistory.todayA: The palace stands inside the Medina of Marrakesh, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in {unescoYear} (no. {unescoRef}). From {protectorate} it served as the residence of the French resident-general.
palaceHistory.todayB: Attendance: {visitors} visitors between January and April {visitorsYear}. No official annual total is published; figures circulating as “500,000 a year” are estimates.
palaceHistory.srcIntro: The palace has a real scholarly literature. These are the works this page draws on, not a link to an encyclopedia summary of them.
palaceHistory.srcFooter: Where these sources disagree, the disagreement is stated rather than resolved silently. The full bibliography, the open questions and the correction policy are on the <link>sources page</link>.

palaceSources.intro: Most of what circulates online about Bahia Palace traces back to the same handful of unsourced tourist pages, copying each other’s dates. This page lists what this site reads instead, and where those readings are uncertain.
palaceSources.citedNote: Deverdun remains the standard survey of Marrakesh before the Protectorate and is the source for the palace’s dated inscriptions. Wilbaux is the reference on how the medina’s built fabric formed. Ghachem-Benkirane and Saharoff document the interiors.
palaceSources.disagreeIntro: These are stated as open rather than resolved in favour of whichever version reads better.
palaceSources.d1: Many sites say {wrongYear}. That is the year Sultan {sultanMuhammad} took the throne, not a construction date. The two chambers flanking the garden carry an inscription dating them to {founded}, which is the earliest firm evidence the building offers about itself.
palaceSources.q2: Was Ba Ahmed the son of a slave?
palaceSources.d2: His grandfather was owned by Sultan {sultanSlimane} and rose to be his chamberlain. His father Si Moussa was already a court officer when Ba Ahmed was born in {birth}, so the widely repeated “slave’s son” is a generation out.
palaceSources.q3: Where does the name come from?
palaceSources.a3: Reportedly from Ba Ahmed’s favourite wife.
palaceSources.d3: al-Bahia means “the brilliant”. Some accounts read the name as describing the palace itself rather than a person. The claim that Ba Ahmed chose it himself as an act of calculated arrogance has nothing behind it and has been removed.
palaceSources.d4: His death year is given variously as the late 1870s and as 1890. The sources do not agree, and this site does not pick one.
palaceSources.q5: How many people visit each year?
palaceSources.d5: The only published count is {visitors} visitors between January and April {visitorsYear}. Figures circulating as “500,000 a year” are estimates, and are labelled as such wherever this site uses them.
palaceSources.methodTitle: How facts get onto this site
palaceSources.m1: Every date, measurement and name about the palace lives in one file and is rendered from it, so two pages cannot quietly disagree the way they used to.
palaceSources.m2: A dated inscription on the building outranks a figure repeated across travel sites, however many repeat it.
palaceSources.m3: A claim that cannot be traced to a named source is removed rather than rounded, softened, or attributed to a plausible-sounding authority.
palaceSources.m4: Where a number is an estimate, the page says so and names what is actually measured.
palaceSources.m5: No translated sentence contains a digit. Numbers are injected into every language from the same file, so a date cannot drift while being translated.
palaceSources.m6: First-hand observation is labelled as the author’s own and never presented as documentary evidence. See the <link>editorial page</link>.
palaceSources.errorBody: Corrections are welcome, particularly from historians, guides and archivists working on Marrakesh. Cite the source you are working from and the page it contradicts, and it will be checked and fixed.

palacePlan.introA: Bahia Palace was built in phases across four decades with no master plan, so it has no symmetry and no single correct route. Most visitors walk a vague loop and leave unsure whether they saw everything. Seven spaces, in the order the circuit takes you.
palacePlan.introB: Tap any block to read what it is, what most people walk past, and what happened there.
palacePlan.drawingA: It is a schematic of sequence and adjacency. It is accurate about the order you meet the spaces and which ones adjoin. It is not a measured plan: the blocks are not scaled, and their proportions are not the real footprints.
palacePlan.drawingB: Measured plans of the palace were published by Gaston Deverdun in 1959. Drawing something that merely looked surveyed would be inventing evidence, so this page does not. The grounds cover {total} hectares including the agdal garden, of which the built palace is nearly {built}.
palacePlan.srcFooter: Full bibliography and the open questions: <link>sources page</link>.
palacePlan.diagramLabel: Schematic plan of Bahia Palace showing seven spaces in visitor order
palacePlan.legendCourt: open courtyard = void inside its gallery
palacePlan.schematicNote: Schematic, not a survey. It is accurate about the order you meet the spaces and which ones adjoin. The blocks are not drawn to scale and their proportions are not the real footprints.
palacePlan.totalTime: Walking the full circuit at this pace: {lo} to {hi} minutes.
palacePlan.s_entrance_summary: Heavy studded doors on Rue Riad Zitoun el Jedid, opening into a narrow, dim corridor.
palacePlan.s_entrance_n0: The ironwork studs and carved frame of the gate itself, which most visitors walk straight past.
palacePlan.s_entrance_n1: The first painted ceiling panel is directly above you in the corridor.
palacePlan.s_entrance_n2: The darkness is deliberate. It makes the first courtyard feel larger than it is.
palacePlan.s_smallriad_summary: The older, quieter courtyard. This is the house before it became a palace.
palacePlan.s_smallriad_n0: The proportions are domestic, not ceremonial. These rooms were lived in.
palacePlan.s_smallriad_n1: The plasterwork is plainer than what comes later, and the floor zellige is in unusually good condition.
palacePlan.s_smallriad_n2: Hold this scale in mind. The contrast with the next courtyard is the sharpest architectural moment in the palace.
palacePlan.s_smallriad_story: This is Si Moussa’s building. The two chambers flanking the garden carry an inscription dating them to {founded}, the earliest firm date anywhere on the site. Everything grander was added by his son thirty years later.
palacePlan.s_grandriad_summary: The centrepiece: a wide courtyard garden ringed by a painted wooden gallery on columns.
palacePlan.s_grandriad_n0: Every panel of the gallery ceiling is different. Look at four in a row and you will see no pattern repeats.
palacePlan.s_grandriad_n1: Crouch. The floor zellige takes on depth at a low angle that it does not have from standing height.
palacePlan.s_grandriad_n2: The marble. It was imported, and it was meant to be noticed.
palacePlan.s_grandriad_story: The marble courtyard carries its own inscription, dated {marble}, in the middle of Ba Ahmed’s six years as the effective ruler of Morocco. He assembled the ground for all of this by absorbing the plots of some {houses} neighbouring houses.
palacePlan.s_greatcourt_summary: The formal reception sequence, where petitioners and foreign envoys were received.
palacePlan.s_greatcourt_n0: Bands of carved Quranic calligraphy run high on the walls, above where anyone naturally looks.
palacePlan.s_greatcourt_n1: The gebs plasterwork is at its finest here, carved so thin it reads as lace.
palacePlan.s_greatcourt_n2: Notice how far into the complex a visitor had to be admitted to stand here. That was the point.
palacePlan.s_greatcourt_story: Ba Ahmed held power from these rooms as grand vizier and regent between {expansion}. Foreign governments dealt with him rather than with the young sultan in whose name he governed.
palacePlan.s_council_summary: The most densely painted ceiling in the palace, above an empty floor.
palacePlan.s_council_n0: Stand underneath it, not in the doorway. The composition only resolves from directly below.
palacePlan.s_council_n1: The blues and reds are mineral pigment and have barely shifted in over a century.
palacePlan.s_council_n2: The emptiness is not neglect. It is the event.
palacePlan.s_council_story: When Ba Ahmed died on {death}, Sultan {sultanYoung} reportedly ordered the palace stripped of its valuables and the household turned out. The ceilings, floors and plaster survived for one reason: they could not be carried away.
palacePlan.s_harem_summary: Living quarters arranged as a hierarchy, with rank measured in distance from the grand riad.
palacePlan.s_harem_n0: The scale drops from ceremonial to human. These were rooms, not stages.
palacePlan.s_harem_n1: Painted tile dados survive in several rooms, and their complexity varies with the status of who lived there.
palacePlan.s_harem_n2: The mashrabiya lattices let the women see out without being seen. Privacy and control in the same screen.
palacePlan.s_harem_story: Rooms nearest the grand riad were the most prestigious. The plan itself records who mattered, which makes this the one part of the palace where the architecture is legible as a social document.
palacePlan.s_gardens_summary: Orange, lemon, cypress, jasmine and rose, laid out on a central axis around water.
palacePlan.s_gardens_n0: The four planting beds follow the traditional four-part Islamic garden scheme.
palacePlan.s_gardens_n1: March and April are when the jasmine and roses carry.
palacePlan.s_gardens_n2: Sit for a quarter of an hour. The medina noise drops away and the palace becomes a different building.
palacePlan.s_gardens_story: The palace proper covers nearly {built} hectares. The {total}-hectare figure quoted everywhere includes the agdal, the walled orchard-garden that the grounds were built around.
